title.value: Analytical Theory of Multiphase Multicomponent Displacement in Porous Media

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Displacement of a multicomponent oil by an injection gas mixture is described by a complex set of material balance equations when more than one phase is present. In order to solve this problem analytically, we assume isothermal one-dimensional flow of components with no dispersion in a homogeneous porous medium. The method of characteristics technique is used to solve the resulting system of quasilinear, non-strictly hyperbolic equations. Phase behavior and composition dependent viscosities are taken into account in the solutions. We also allow the total flow velocity to vary due to the volume change (VC) that occurs upon mixing of components when they transfer between the phases. We also include the solutions without volumetric effects to show the impact of the assumption of no volume change on mixing (NVC), which is frequently made in the analysis of compositional processes.A decoupling technique is developed to obtain the total velocity term for the solutions with VC. New solution tools are developed for multicomponent displacements using generalized tie lines in the concentration space. An alternative formulation is developed to examine the sharpening behavior of variations along nontie-line paths and to select the appropriate velocities for self-sharpening waves. Equal eigenvalue points (path switch points) on a tie line as well as all the eigenvalues along a tie line are obtained based on single point calculations. The behavior of the equal eigenvalue points is linked to the alternative formulation, where a tie-line envelope concept is used.Binary and ternary example solutions are studied in detail for VC and NVC cases. Injection of different gases is considered at the same injection density level. Phase behavior alone is found to be the most important factor for those gas injections. Both vaporizing and condensing gas drives are observed. All the vaporizing gas drives showed self-sharpening behavior in the two-phase region while the condensing gas drive showed spreading behavior in the two-phase region. Effect of pressure on the pure C02 injections indicated the same trend as the slim-tube experiments in the literature when VC is considered. The slope of the recovery curve before breakthrough is found to be the convective velocity term just at the downstream of the leading shock. One well defined experiment from the literature is also compared with the method of characteristics solutions. Other important features of the example solutions are also addressed.A complete classification of the four component systems is also made. Based on that classification, development of miscibility is explained for each case. Some of the solutions are also compared with the solutions with NVC. The four component examples are compared with finite difference solutions. For the finite difference solutions, a new scheme is developed to calculate the the total flow velocity in the absence of pressure equation. A set of experimental data is compared with quaternary method of characteristics solutions.Most of the new concepts introduced here are used to perform a complete analysis for systems with constant equilibrium ratios (k-values). Special attention is given to the explanation of the sharpening behavior of the nontie-line paths. The simplified model for constant k-values is used to establish the foundations for multicomponent systems.The main focus of this research is Riemann problems where initial data consist of two constant states in composition space. A simple case using a nonuniform initial data for the classical Buckley-Leverett problem is also studied in detail. The procedure used can also be applied for slug injection processes.
Dindoruk, Birol. (1992). Analytical Theory of Multiphase Multicomponent Displacement in Porous Media. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/mg945kw6130
